newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian finance industry cuts growth estimate.
newsitem.headline: Colombian finance industry cuts growth estimate.

text.p: Colombia's influential National Association of Financial Institutions (ANIF) has cut its 1996 economic growth estimate by half a percentage point, citing the rise in urban unemployment and crisis in the key coffee sector as signs of the depth of recession.
In its weekly report issued at the weekend, ANIF revised its original estimate of 3 percent growth to 2.5 percent, a full point lower than the government's target of 3.5 percent.
"Unemployment is rising because those sectors that traditionally generate job opportunities, such as coffee, industry, construction and trade are very sluggish," the ANIF report said.
"On the demand side the most worrying factors are the slow growth in consumer spending, demonstrated by the fall in retail sales, and the fall of exports in real terms," it said.

According to National Statistics Department figures released Thursday, Colombia's urban unemployment rate stood at 12.1 percent of the workforce in September, against 8.7 percent in September last year.

ANIF estimated the 1996-97 coffee crop would be 11.6 percent lower than the preliminary figure of 12.9 million 60-kg sacks which Jorge Cardenas, head of the National Federation of Coffee Growers, estimated for the 1995-96 harvest in a statement Friday.

The ANIF weekly report also criticized the deal hammered out between the government, private transport companies and truck drivers Thursday, which ended the strike that virtually paralyzed the national economy for 11 days.

It described the agreement as a "fragile accord", which it said could push cargo freight rates up by as much as 35 percent by early next year after an inflation-indexed rise is added to the immediate 16 percent raise agreed by the Colombian Truck Drivers' Association and the Transport Ministry.

ANIF said cargo freight rates had been forced down by the law of the free market, given that there was an oversupply of transport services. Truck drivers leaders said the raise would not fuel inflation because transport companies would accept reduced profit margins.
